item.title: Federal judge blocks attempts to restrict mail-in voting
item.description: AUGUSTA, MAINE – A federal judge in Boston blocked the Trump administration from interfering with states’ rights to conduct mail-in voting for the upcoming November elections, now 67 days away. Judge Indira Talwani ruled yesterday that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed in proving the administration’s order was unconstitutional. “Last night’s decision was wonderful news for Maine voters who rely on absentee voting,” Secretary Bellows said . “The judge made clear that the states, not the federal government, are in charge of elections. That goes to the heart of our legal fights in court against the Trump Administration. We will continue to stand with other states and voting rights advocates across the nation to defend the voting rights – including the right to vote by mail – for every citizen.” In the decision, Judge Talwani wrote, “the Constitution charges the States with election administration” going on to say that no law has been passed by Congress that “would permit the USPS to regulate election mail.” The judge went even further to note that with just two months to the election, it would an expensive and likely impossible task for the 2026 election, saying, “Plaintiff States face irreparable harm where they are required to comply with a likely unconstitutional regulation for which compliance is practically impossible.” ### Attachment: read the 08-27-26 order
item.content:encoded:
AUGUSTA, MAINE – A federal judge in Boston blocked the Trump administration from interfering with states’ rights to conduct mail-in voting for the upcoming November elections, now 67 days away. Judge Indira Talwani ruled yesterday that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed in proving the administration’s order was unconstitutional. 

“Last night’s decision was wonderful news for Maine voters who rely on absentee voting,” Secretary Bellows said. “The judge made clear that the states, not the federal government, are in charge of elections. That goes to the heart of our legal fights in court against the Trump Administration. We will continue to stand with other states and voting rights advocates across the nation to defend the voting rights – including the right to vote by mail – for every citizen.”

In the decision, Judge Talwani wrote, “the Constitution charges the States with election administration” going on to say that no law has been passed by Congress that “would permit the USPS to regulate election mail.” The judge went even further to note that with just two months to the election, it would an expensive and likely impossible task for the 2026 election, saying, “Plaintiff States face irreparable harm where they are required to comply with a likely unconstitutional regulation for which compliance is practically impossible.” 

###

Argued March 31, 2026—Decided May 28, 2026 In 2004, two black teenagers, Terry Pitchford and Eric Bullins, robbed a grocery store near Grenada, Mississippi. During the robbery, Bullins shot and killed the white store owner. Bullins reached a plea agree- ment and received a 20-year sentence for the homicide. The State charged Pitchford with capital murder and sought the death penalty. During jury selection at Pitchford's trial, the prosecutor used peremp- tory strikes against four of the fve black potential jurors. As this Court held in Batson v. Kentucky, 476 U. S. 79, the Equal Protection Clause bars prosecutors from exercising peremptory challenges based on race. In Batson and subsequent cases, the Court has spelled out a three-step process for a trial court to determine whether a prosecutor employed a peremptory challenge based on race. Here, Pitchford's counsel raised an objection under Batson and made a prima facie show- ing that the strikes of the four black jurors were based on race (step one). The trial court asked the prosecutor for race-neutral reasons for each strike, and the prosecutor offered reasons (step two). Argued November 12, 2025—Decided May 28, 2026* Petitioner Daniel Rutherford was convicted of two counts of using and carrying a frearm during a crime of violence, in violation of 18 U. S. C. § 924(c). Petitioner Johnnie Carter was convicted of three § 924(c) viola- tions. At the time each was sentenced, a defendant convicted of two § 924(c) counts was subject to a mandatory 25-year sentence for the sec- ond offense that would be “stacked” upon (i. e., run consecutively to) the frst offense's mandatory penalty. That sentencing scheme resulted in a 32-year minimum sentence for Rutherford's § 924(c) violations and a 57-year minimum sentence for Carter's violations. Years later, Con- gress passed the First Step Act of 2018, which eliminated the 25-year stacking requirement for frst-time offenders. Rutherford and Carter do not qualify for the Act's reduced penalties because the amendment to § 924(c) does not apply to defendants sentenced before the Act. item.description:
STATE OF MAINE APPELLATE DIVISON WORKERS’ COMPENSATION BOARD Case No. App. Div. 25-0013 Decision No. 26-08
TAMMIE L. (COOMBS) KILLAM (Appellee)
v.
MAINEHEALTH (Appellant)
and
SYNERNET (Insurer)
Conference held: April 8, 2026 Decided: August 27, 2026
PANEL MEMBERS: Administrative Law Judges Stovall, Rooks, and Smith By: Administrative Law Judge Smith
[¶1] MaineHealth/Maine Coast Memorial Hospital (the Hospital) appeals from a decision of a Workers’ Compensation Board administrative law judge (Hirtle, ALJ) denying the Hospital’s Petition for Review pertaining to Tammie Killam’s July 2, 2014 , work injury. The Hospital co ntends the ALJ erred by interpreting the independent medical examiner’s (IME’S) opinion to contain an “unambiguous” assessment of no work capacity , and by adopting that interpretation . We disagree and affirm the decision. I. BACKGROUND [¶2] Tammie Killam was hired by the Hospital as a full -time orderly on October 21, 2013. On July 2, 2014, while moving a table in the operating room, she 2
felt and heard a pop on the ulnar side of her let wrist. As established in a consent decree dated March 7, 2018 , Ms. Killam sustained a work-related left wrist injury on July 2, 2014, and resulting “psychological overlay consistent with an adjustment disorder with depression and anxiety.” The parties agreed she was entitled to receive total incapacity benefits without prejudice, pursuant to 39-A M.R.S.A. § 212. [¶3] In 2020, the Hospital filed a Petition for Review and sought to reduce Ms. Killam’s level of benefits to reflect a full-time, minimum wage -earning capacity. Ms. Killam then filed a Petition for Payment of Medical and Related Services.
